title: Philip of Macedon
objective: After this level you can explain how Philip conquered the Greek cities.
summary: Philip II, once a hostage in Thebes, built an army around the long sarissa, beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, and was murdered in 336 BCE.

cards.headline: A hostage from Macedonia grew up to become master of Greece.
cards.body: As a young man, Philip was held in Thebes. In 338 BCE he beat Thebes and Athens in a single battle. What did he learn in between?

cards.headline: Schooled by the enemy
cards.body: Around 367 BCE, Philip, a young prince of Macedonia, was sent to Thebes as a hostage and stayed about three years. He used the time well: he studied under Epaminondas, Thebes’ great general. In 359 BCE, at 23, Philip became king of Macedonia. Imagine a rival team’s coach giving you private lessons, then sending you home.

cards.headline: A longer reach
cards.body: Philip rebuilt his army around the sarissa, a pike nearly one and a half times as long as the spear other Greeks carried. Think of a shoving match where your opponent’s pole is half again as long as yours: his point reaches you before yours reaches him. Greek armies were about to find out how that felt.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing about Philip, make it the sarissa: his point reached you first.

cards.fact: In 338 BCE Philip beat Athens and Thebes together at Chaeronea.
cards.context: His son Alexander, only 18, commanded the left wing. Remember Level 2’s Athens and Thebes, less than 100 km apart yet foreign rivals? They finally fought side by side, and lost side by side. In 337 BCE Philip gathered the Greek states into the League of Corinth, with himself as leader, and planned a war on Persia.

cards.headline: The war he never fought
cards.body: Philip never reached Persia. In 336 BCE, during celebrations of his daughter’s wedding in the theater at Aegae, his own bodyguard Pausanias stabbed him to death. Alexander, born in 356 BCE, became king at 20. He inherited the army, the league and the plan.

questions.prompt: What was the sarissa that Philip of Macedon gave his soldiers?

options.label: A short curved sword for close fighting
A pike half again as long as a Greek spear
A bronze shield wide enough for two men
options.rationale: It was a pike, not a shield.

options.label: A light javelin thrown before a charge
options.rationale: It was held, and it was long.

questions.explanation: The sarissa was a pike nearly one and a half times as long as the Greek spear, so Philip’s men reached the enemy first.

questions.prompt: What did young Philip gain from his years as a hostage in Thebes?

options.label: The throne of Thebes
options.rationale: He became king of Macedonia, not Thebes.

options.label: A marriage alliance with Athens
options.rationale: The card says nothing of a marriage.

options.label: Lessons from the Theban general Epaminondas
Nothing, since he was locked in a cell
options.rationale: He studied while he was there.

questions.explanation: In Thebes, Philip studied under the great general Epaminondas, then came home to build a new army.

questions.prompt: Level 2’s rival cities, Athens and Thebes, finally fought on the same side in 338 BCE. How did it go?

options.label: They beat Philip and freed Macedonia
They lost together to Philip at Chaeronea
They conquered Persia side by side
They split up before the battle began

questions.explanation: At Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip defeated Athens and Thebes together.
